claim: Humans only use 10% of their brains.
search_phrase: do we only use 10 percent of our brain
evidence_summary: Brain-damage, imaging and metabolic evidence reviewed in BMJ contradict the literal 10% claim; this does not mean every brain region is equally active at every moment.

attribution.origin: The first author of this widespread belief is not established here. It must not be attributed to Albert Einstein: the cited review says no such recorded statement by him has been found.
attribution.documentedAppearance: Rachel C. Vreeman and Aaron E. Carroll document and critically review the assertion “We use only 10% of our brains” in Medical myths (BMJ, 2007). They are reviewers of the myth, not its original claimants.

analysis.text: The claim asserts that most of the brain is unused. Vreeman and Carroll’s review describes evidence from brain damage, brain imaging, localisation of function, microstructural analysis and metabolism showing that people use much more than ten percent. These are different ways of investigating brain function, not repeated votes by AI engines.

The brain-damage evidence matters because damage to almost any region can have specific lasting effects on mental, bodily and behavioural abilities. The imaging and metabolic evidence described in the review does not reveal a permanently dormant ninety percent. Together, these observations contradict the premise that most brain tissue has no functioning role.

This verdict does not imply that all neurons fire simultaneously, that each region is equally busy, or that people cannot learn new skills. Activity depends on the task and the time of observation. The popular self-improvement interpretation of “untapped potential” is different from a literal claim that ninety percent of the brain is unused.

The review notes that the belief persisted for over a century and discusses an earlier literature review of its origins. It also warns that the Einstein attribution has no recorded statement behind it. We have not independently traced the first publication, so the historical origin remains unknown rather than being assigned to a famous person.

review.limitations: This is a dated editorial reading of one peer-reviewed narrative review, not a new systematic neuroscience review or an individual brain assessment. The historical references cited by that article have not all been independently examined. The finding addresses literal brain use, not a numerical measure of human potential.

sources.title: Medical myths
sources.authors: Rachel C. Vreeman and Aaron E. Carroll
sources.quote: Numerous types of brain imaging studies show that no area of the brain is completely silent or inactive.
sources.relevance: The review draws together brain-damage, imaging, localisation and metabolic findings rather than treating the popularity of the saying as evidence. Its discussion explicitly addresses the literal ten-percent assertion.

claim: The Great Wall of China is visible from space with the naked eye.
search_phrase: is the great wall of china visible from space
evidence_summary: NASA says the Wall is not visible from the Moon and is difficult or impossible to see from Earth orbit without the high-powered lenses used for its photograph. The broad naked-eye claim needs this distance and viewing-condition qualification.

attribution.origin: The original claimant and first publication of this popular myth are not established by the available NASA source. NASA is documenting and correcting the assertion, not claiming authorship of it.
attribution.documentedAppearance: NASA’s Great Wall image article (April 2, 2009) explicitly refers to “myths to the contrary” when explaining the Moon and Earth-orbit visibility claims.

analysis.text: NASA’s image article shows why an orbital photograph does not establish the naked-eye claim. The image was taken by Expedition 10 Commander Leroy Chiao on the International Space Station, and the explanatory text explicitly identifies the high-powered lenses used. A photograph taken with magnification is not equivalent to unaided human vision.

The source distinguishes two cases: the Wall is not visible from the Moon, while seeing it from Earth orbit is described as difficult or impossible without the high-powered lenses. The word “space” in the original assertion does not specify distance, altitude or observing conditions. That ambiguity matters: the Moon and low Earth orbit are not interchangeable viewpoints.

The contradicted label rejects the broad, unqualified naked-eye assertion. It is not a claim that no observer could ever identify any section under any exceptional orbital conditions. NASA’s own cautious wording is retained instead of converting “difficult or impossible” into an unsupported universal prohibition.

The NASA page is a documented institutional discussion of the myth, with an identifiable image and publication date. It does not identify the person who first spread the claim. We therefore link the correction and explicitly leave the first claimant unknown; the astronaut associated with the photograph is not presented as the originator of the myth.

review.limitations: The evidence is NASA’s explanation of one published image, not a controlled survey of every orbital observation. It does not settle all exceptional lighting, altitude or eyesight cases, nor establish the first historical publication. Distinguish naked-eye viewing, magnified photography and Moon-distance viewing.

sources.title: Great Wall
sources.quote: Despite myths to the contrary, the wall isn’t visible from the moon, and is difficult or impossible to see from Earth orbit without the high-powered lenses used for this photo.
sources.relevance: NASA explains the viewing conditions of a specific International Space Station photograph by Expedition 10 Commander Leroy Chiao. It directly distinguishes a camera image taken with high-powered lenses from naked-eye observation.

claim: Lightning is hotter than the surface of the Sun.
search_phrase: is lightning hotter than the sun
evidence_summary: Lightning reaches ~30,000°C, about 5x hotter than the Sun's surface (~5,500°C) per NOAA.

claim: Water drains in the opposite direction in the Southern Hemisphere.
search_phrase: which way does water drain in australia
evidence_summary: The Coriolis effect is far too weak at sink/toilet scale; drain direction is set by basin shape and water flow.

claim: Earth's seasons are caused by its distance from the Sun.
evidence_summary: NASA explains that seasonal weather patterns are mainly caused by Earth’s 23.5-degree axial tilt, not the elliptical orbit. Earth is near the Sun in January while the Northern Hemisphere is in winter.

attribution.origin: No original person or first publication responsible for this misconception is established by the cited material. It is reviewed as a general causal assertion, not attributed to a named speaker.
attribution.documentedAppearance: NASA Goddard’s StarChild question “When is Earth closest to the Sun?” (January 2003) explicitly asks whether varying Earth–Sun distance causes seasons and explains why it does not.

analysis.text: NASA’s StarChild explanation identifies the 23.5-degree tilt of Earth’s spin axis as the main cause of seasonal weather patterns. The causal claim being reviewed is that changing distance from the Sun produces the seasons. The source directly contrasts that explanation with axial tilt rather than merely stating that Earth’s orbit is elliptical.

During northern winter, the north pole is tilted away from the Sun and days are shorter. NASA explains that being a little closer to the Sun in January does not make much difference to that seasonal pattern. This is a useful check on the distance explanation: proximity alone would not explain why northern winter occurs near that point in the orbit.

At the same time, the Southern Hemisphere has the opposite seasonal pattern because the south pole is tilted toward the Sun during northern winter. Keeping the hemispheric distinction is essential. “January is winter” is not a globally valid statement, and a source about Northern Hemisphere winter cannot be used as if it describes both hemispheres.

The cited page is a January 2003 educational question with a year-specific perihelion example. We do not turn its exact calendar date into a permanent annual rule. The conclusion is about the principal cause of the seasonal cycle, not a claim that orbital distance has absolutely no effect on the energy Earth receives.

review.limitations: This is an editorial review of NASA’s educational explanation, not a detailed climate model. The page’s calendar example is historical and its wording is “mostly caused”; the review does not assert that Earth–Sun distance has zero physical effect. The first historical author of the misconception remains unestablished.

sources.title: When is Earth closest to the Sun?
sources.publisher: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / StarChild
sources.quote: Seasonal weather patterns are mostly caused by the 23.5-degree tilt of our planet's spin axis and not by Earth's elliptical orbit.
sources.relevance: NASA’s educational explanation directly addresses the proposed cause of seasons and contrasts the simultaneous Northern and Southern Hemisphere seasons. Its historical perihelion example is explicitly about 2003.

claim: Old window glass is thicker at the bottom because glass is a slow-flowing liquid.
evidence_summary: Glass is an amorphous solid. Old panes vary due to historic manufacturing, not flow.

claim: The Moon has a permanently dark side.
evidence_summary: NASA StarChild explains that the far side receives as much sunlight as the near side. A hemisphere hidden from Earth is not permanently unlit.

attribution.origin: The first claimant and first publication are unknown here. NASA documents the popular phrase but is not presented as its original author.
attribution.documentedAppearance: NASA Goddard's StarChild Team explicitly discusses the phrase 'dark side of the Moon' in The Dark Side of the Moon. The retrieved page has no established publication date; it is a documented explanation, not proof of the phrase's historical origin.

analysis.text: The reviewed claim is about a permanently dark hemisphere, not merely the hemisphere hidden from an Earth-based observer. NASA distinguishes these meanings explicitly: the unseen hemisphere is more accurately called the far side. Being out of our view does not mean being out of sunlight.

NASA's explanation states that the side we do not see from Earth receives just as much sunlight as the side we see. That directly contradicts the unqualified permanent-darkness assertion. The relevant distinction is illumination by the Sun versus visibility from Earth; those are different observing geometries.

The source explains that the dark side at a given time is the side pointed away from the Sun. This is a temporary illumination condition rather than a fixed hemisphere. The verdict therefore rejects the literal permanent-dark-side claim while retaining the ordinary use of far side for the hemisphere facing away from Earth.

review.limitations: This is an editorial reading of NASA's educational explanation, verified through the existing cached page-extraction provider on October 30, 2026, not a new lunar illumination study. It concerns hemispheres, not every local crater or permanently shadowed polar region. No first historical claimant or publication date for the NASA page was established.

sources.title: The Dark Side of the Moon
sources.publisher: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / StarChild
sources.quote: The side of the Moon we do not see from Earth gets just as much sunlight on it as the side we do see.
sources.relevance: The excerpt was found verbatim in the live cached PageExtractionProvider output; NASA directly distinguishes the far side from permanent darkness.

claim: Daddy longlegs are the most venomous spiders but their fangs can't pierce skin.
evidence_summary: They lack venom glands entirely; they aren't even true spiders (they're opiliones).

claim: You can't fold a piece of paper more than 7 times.
search_phrase: how many times can you fold paper
evidence_summary: High school students folded toilet paper 12+ times in 2002; MythBusters folded a giant sheet 11 times.

claim: A penny dropped from a skyscraper can kill someone.
search_phrase: penny dropped from empire state building
evidence_summary: A penny's terminal velocity (~50 km/h) is too low; it would sting at most, per physicist calculations.

claim: Bats are blind.
evidence_summary: All bat species can see; many see well and also use echolocation.

claim: Goldfish have a 3-second memory.
evidence_summary: Studies show goldfish remember feeding routines and mazes for months.

claim: Chameleons change color to blend in with their surroundings.
evidence_summary: Color change primarily regulates temperature and communicates mood; camouflage is secondary.

claim: Lemmings commit mass suicide by jumping off cliffs.
evidence_summary: A 1958 Disney documentary staged this. Lemmings migrate and can drown crossing rivers, but never suicide.

claim: Ostriches bury their heads in the sand when scared.
evidence_summary: They lower their heads to tend eggs or scan; the myth likely comes from their camouflage posture seen from afar.

claim: Bulls attack because they hate the color red.
search_phrase: do bulls hate the color red
evidence_summary: Cattle are red-green colorblind; they react to the matador's movement, not the cape color.

claim: Different parts of the tongue taste different flavors.
evidence_summary: All taste regions detect all five tastes; the 'map' is a misreading of a 1901 paper.

claim: Humans have exactly five senses.
search_phrase: how many senses do humans have
evidence_summary: Scientists count 20+ including proprioception, balance, temperature, and pain.

claim: Hair and fingernails keep growing after death.
evidence_summary: Skin dehydrates and retracts, making them look longer. Growth requires living tissue.

claim: The tongue is the strongest muscle in the body.
evidence_summary: Strength depends on how you measure it; the tongue is actually 8 muscles and no metric crowns it strongest.

claim: Pure water is a good conductor of electricity.
evidence_summary: Pure (distilled) water is a poor conductor; dissolved minerals make tap water conductive.

claim: Mars is red because its surface is literally rusty.
evidence_summary: Iron oxide (rust) dust covers the surface, giving Mars its color per NASA.

claim: Natural diamonds are formed from compressed coal.
evidence_summary: Diamonds form from carbon in the mantle (likely carbonate rocks, not coal) under extreme heat and pressure.

claim: Shaving makes hair grow back thicker and darker.
evidence_summary: Cut hair has a blunt tip that feels coarse; the follicle is unaffected (Mayo Clinic).

claim: Cracking your knuckles causes arthritis.
evidence_summary: A long-term study of a chronic knuckle-cracker found no arthritis link; the sound is gas bubbles popping.

claim: Eating sugar makes children hyperactive.
evidence_summary: Double-blind studies show no behavioral effect; the excitement is usually the occasion (parties), not the sugar.

claim: Vaccines cause autism.
evidence_summary: Large studies of millions of children found no link. The 1998 Wakefield paper was fraudulent and retracted.

claim: The flu shot can give you the flu.
search_phrase: can the flu shot give you the flu
evidence_summary: CDC states that flu vaccines cannot cause flu illness: injected vaccines use inactivated viruses or a single viral protein. Side effects and infections acquired around vaccination are different from vaccine-caused flu.

attribution.origin: The first speaker or publication responsible for this misconception is not established. CDC is a documented institutional reviewer of the assertion, not its original claimant.
attribution.documentedAppearance: CDC's Misconceptions About Seasonal Flu and Flu Vaccines, dated September 6, 2024, addresses the assertion under 'Getting a flu vaccine will not give you flu'.

analysis.text: CDC directly states that flu vaccines cannot cause flu illness. Its explanation identifies the material in injected flu vaccines as either inactivated viruses or a single protein from an influenza virus. The reviewed assertion is that the shot causes influenza infection, not that vaccination can have no adverse effects.

CDC separately describes soreness, redness, tenderness or swelling after a shot and possible low-grade fever, headache and muscle aches. These reactions are not evidence that the injected vaccine gave someone influenza. Keeping side effects separate from flu illness avoids replacing the misconception with an equally inaccurate claim that reactions never happen.

The same source explains why someone may become ill after vaccination: exposure shortly before vaccination or during the roughly two-week period needed for protection, another respiratory virus, imperfect vaccine effectiveness or a mismatch with circulating influenza viruses. A later infection does not by itself establish that the shot caused it.

The source acknowledges rare serious allergic reactions and variation in effectiveness. The contradicted verdict is deliberately narrow: it addresses vaccine-caused influenza, not guaranteed protection against every respiratory illness or a universal assessment of an individual's eligibility for vaccination.

review.limitations: This review uses one dated CDC public-health explanation, with short excerpts verified through the existing cached page-extraction provider on October 30, 2026. It is not an independent systematic review, a diagnosis or individual medical advice. The historical origin of the misconception remains unknown; symptoms and suitability should be discussed with a qualified clinician.

sources.relevance: Verified verbatim in the cached PageExtractionProvider output. The surrounding CDC explanation distinguishes injected vaccine ingredients, side effects, imperfect protection and respiratory infections acquired around vaccination.

claim: Being out in cold weather makes you catch a cold.
search_phrase: does cold weather make you sick
evidence_summary: Colds are caused by viruses. Cold, dry air may help viruses survive and spread, but temperature alone doesn't cause illness.

claim: Eating carrots dramatically improves your eyesight.
evidence_summary: Vitamin A deficiency damages vision, so carrots help only if you're deficient; they won't give you better-than-normal vision.

claim: Turkey makes you sleepy because of tryptophan.
evidence_summary: Turkey has no more tryptophan than chicken or cheese; the post-meal drowsiness is from overeating and alcohol.

claim: Microwaving food destroys its nutrients.
evidence_summary: Microwaving often preserves nutrients BETTER than boiling because of shorter cook times and less water.

claim: MSG (monosodium glutamate) is dangerous to eat.
evidence_summary: The FDA classifies MSG as generally safe. Self-reported sensitivity exists, but controlled studies find no consistent harm.

claim: Everyone must drink exactly 8 glasses of water a day.
search_phrase: how much water should you drink a day
evidence_summary: Needs vary with body size, activity, and climate; food also provides water. 8 glasses is a rough guideline, not a rule.

claim: Vitamin C prevents the common cold.
evidence_summary: For the general population it doesn't prevent colds; regular use may slightly shorten their duration.

claim: Sitting too close to the TV damages your eyes.
search_phrase: does sitting close to the tv hurt your eyes
evidence_summary: It causes temporary eye strain at most; no permanent damage. Kids sit close because they can focus closer.

claim: Detox diets and juice cleanses remove toxins from your body.
evidence_summary: Your liver and kidneys detox continuously; no product has been shown to remove named 'toxins.'

claim: Antibiotics can cure viral infections like colds and flu.
evidence_summary: Antibiotics kill bacteria only; taking them for viruses drives resistance with zero benefit.

claim: Going outside with wet hair in winter makes you sick.
search_phrase: going outside with wet hair sick
evidence_summary: Illness comes from viruses, not cold hair. You may feel chilly, but you won't 'catch' anything.

claim: Drinking alcohol kills brain cells.
evidence_summary: Heavy drinking damages dendrites and impairs function, but doesn't kill neurons outright.

claim: Coffee stunts children's growth.
evidence_summary: No study links caffeine to reduced height; the myth likely came from old ads for a rival drink.

claim: Swallowed chewing gum takes 7 years to digest.
search_phrase: how long does gum take to digest
evidence_summary: Gum passes through the digestive tract in days like other indigestible material.

claim: Einstein failed math in school.
evidence_summary: Einstein was a strong math student, mastering calculus by 15. He objected to rote schooling, not math.

claim: Napoleon Bonaparte was extremely short.
evidence_summary: At ~1.68m he was average or above-average for Frenchmen of his era; British propaganda created the 'tiny tyrant' image.

claim: Vikings wore horned helmets.
evidence_summary: No Viking helmet with horns has ever been found; the image comes from 19th-century opera costumes.

claim: People in the Middle Ages believed the Earth was flat.
search_phrase: did people think the earth was flat
evidence_summary: Educated medieval Europeans knew the Earth was spherical; the myth was invented in the 1800s.

claim: Columbus proved the Earth was round.
search_phrase: did columbus prove the earth is round
evidence_summary: Scholars had known Earth's shape for ~2,000 years (Eratosthenes measured it in 240 BC); Columbus actually underestimated its size.

claim: The Egyptian pyramids were built by slaves.
evidence_summary: Archaeological evidence shows paid, well-fed laborers — paid workers even went on strike over wages.

claim: The Salem 'witches' were burned at the stake.
evidence_summary: Nineteen were hanged, one was pressed to death; none were burned. Burning was a European practice.

claim: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
evidence_summary: Pyramid (~2560 BC) to Cleopatra (~30 BC) ≈ 2,500 years; Cleopatra to Apollo 11 (1969) ≈ 2,000 years.

claim: Europeans first reached America in 1492.
evidence_summary: Norse settlers reached Newfoundland (~1000 AD), centuries before Columbus — though indigenous peoples were there far earlier.

claim: Walt Disney was cryogenically frozen after death.
evidence_summary: Disney was cremated in 1966; the first human cryopreservation happened a month later, unconnected to him.

claim: People swallow an average of 8 spiders a year in their sleep.
search_phrase: do we swallow spiders in our sleep
evidence_summary: No documented case exists; spiders avoid vibrations, breath, and heartbeat. It was likely invented to show how myths spread.

claim: You lose most of your body heat through your head.
search_phrase: do you lose most heat through your head
evidence_summary: Heat loss is proportional to exposed surface area; a bare head loses no more than a bare arm of similar size.

claim: Feeding bread to ducks is harmless.
evidence_summary: Bread causes 'angel wing' deformity and malnutrition; wildlife groups recommend peas, oats, or birdseed instead.

claim: Only 300 Spartans fought at Thermopylae.
evidence_summary: Herodotus reports several thousand Greeks from multiple city-states; 300 was the Spartan royal guard contingent.

claim: Honey never spoils — archaeologists have tasted 3,000-year-old honey.
evidence_summary: Honey's low water content, acidity, and hydrogen peroxide make it hostile to microbes; sealed Egyptian honey was found edible.

claim: A day on Venus is longer than a year on Venus.
evidence_summary: Venus rotates once every 243 Earth days but orbits the Sun in 225 Earth days.

claim: You must carry a credit card balance to build credit.
search_phrase: do you need to carry a balance to build credit
evidence_summary: On-time payments build credit; carrying a balance just costs you interest.

claim: A raise can push you into a higher tax bracket and leave you with less take-home pay.
search_phrase: can a raise lower your paycheck
evidence_summary: Only income ABOVE the bracket threshold is taxed at the higher rate; a raise always increases net pay.

claim: Billionaires legally pay zero income tax.
evidence_summary: Most pay some tax, but effective rates can be far below salary earners due to unrealized gains and capital gains rules (per ProPublica 2021 leak analysis).

claim: You need a lot of money to start investing.
search_phrase: how much money do you need to start investing
evidence_summary: Fractional shares and index funds let you start with a few dollars on mainstream apps.

claim: All debt is bad and should be avoided.
evidence_summary: High-interest consumer debt is harmful; mortgages and low-interest loans can build wealth. It's about interest rate vs. return.

claim: Renting is always throwing money away compared to buying.
evidence_summary: Buying has hidden costs (taxes, maintenance, interest); in some markets and timeframes renting + investing the difference wins.

claim: Using credit cards always hurts your finances.
evidence_summary: Carried balances at high interest are costly; paid-in-full cards build credit and offer rewards with no interest.

claim: Fortune cookies are a traditional Chinese invention.
search_phrase: where do fortune cookies come from
evidence_summary: They originated with Japanese-American bakers in early 1900s California and became a Chinese-restaurant staple in the US.

claim: Sushi means raw fish.
evidence_summary: 'Sushi' refers to vinegared rice; sashimi is the raw fish. Many sushi rolls contain no raw fish at all.

claim: Food picked up within 5 seconds is safe to eat.
evidence_summary: Bacteria transfer instantly on contact; studies show floors deposit microbes within milliseconds of touching.

claim: Swallowing a watermelon seed will grow a watermelon in your stomach.
search_phrase: what happens if you swallow a watermelon seed
evidence_summary: Seeds pass through undigested; stomach acid and the absence of soil/sunlight make growth impossible.

claim: NASA invented Velcro (and Teflon, and the microwave).
evidence_summary: Velcro was patented by Swiss engineer Georges de Mestral in 1955; NASA merely popularized it. Teflon (1938) and microwaves (1945) predate NASA too.

claim: Using a mobile phone at a gas station can trigger an explosion.
search_phrase: can phones cause gas station fires
evidence_summary: No confirmed case exists; the real ignition risk is static electricity from getting in and out of your car.

claim: Incognito mode makes you anonymous on the internet.
evidence_summary: Incognito only stops local history saving; your ISP, employer, and websites still see everything you do.

claim: Adding more RAM always makes a slow computer fast.
search_phrase: will more ram speed up my computer
evidence_summary: RAM helps only if you're memory-limited; a slow HDD or old CPU won't be fixed by extra RAM.

claim: Charging your phone overnight destroys the battery.
evidence_summary: Modern phones stop charging at 100%; heat is the real battery killer, so avoid covered/hot charging spots.

claim: 5G mobile networks are harmful to health at normal exposure levels.
evidence_summary: WHO and ICNIRP state that within international exposure limits, 5G (non-ionizing radiation) has no confirmed health effects.
